title: Sample Space and Probability
source: Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis, Introduction to Probability, MIT course 6.041–6.431, Fall 2000 lecture notes

steps.title: Notation
steps.objective: Read the symbols used in probability before working with the concepts.

steps.title: Sets and events
steps.objective: Recognize events and translate “and”, “or” and “not” into sets.

steps.title: Building a probability model
steps.objective: Choose a suitable sample space and apply the probability axioms.

steps.title: Calculating event probabilities
steps.objective: Use counting, complements, overlap corrections and geometric probability.

steps.title: Conditional probability
steps.objective: Restrict the sample space and multiply conditional probabilities.

steps.title: Total probability and Bayes’ rule
steps.objective: Combine scenarios and update their probabilities after observing evidence.

steps.title: Independence
steps.objective: Distinguish independence, disjointness and conditional independence.

steps.title: Independent trials and reliability
steps.objective: Calculate sequence, binomial and simple system probabilities.

steps.title: Counting
steps.objective: Choose the right count for ordered selections, groups and repeated objects.

questions.question: Ω
questions.correct_answer: The sample space
questions.explanation: Ω is the set of all possible outcomes; it is the universal set for the model.

questions.correct_answer: The empty set
questions.explanation: ∅ has no elements. The symbol Ø is also sometimes used for the empty set.

options: An ordered sequence that must occur in that order
questions.correct_answer: A set containing 1, 2 and 3
questions.explanation: Braces list set elements; their order does not matter.

questions.question: x ∈ A
options: x is a subset of A
x equals the probability of A
x is an element of A
questions.correct_answer: x is an element of A
questions.explanation: ∈ expresses membership of an element in a set.

questions.question: x ∉ A
options: x is a subset of A
x is not an element of A
questions.correct_answer: x is not an element of A
questions.explanation: ∉ negates membership; it says nothing about whether A is empty.

questions.question: A ⊆ B
options: A and B have no common elements
Every element of A is also in B; equality is allowed
A and B must be different sets
A is one element of B
questions.correct_answer: Every element of A is also in B; equality is allowed
questions.explanation: Every element of A is in B, and equality is allowed.

questions.question: B ⊇ A
options: B has strictly more elements than A
B contains every element of A
B contains no element of A
B belongs to A as one element
questions.correct_answer: B contains every element of A
questions.explanation: This is the reverse way to write A ⊆ B; equality is allowed.

questions.question: A ∪ B
options: Only outcomes in both A and B
Outcomes in A or B, including those in both
Outcomes in neither A nor B
Outcomes in exactly one of A and B
questions.correct_answer: Outcomes in A or B, including those in both
questions.explanation: Union uses inclusive “or”: shared outcomes are included.

questions.question: A ∩ B
options: Outcomes in at least one of A and B
Outcomes in both A and B
Outcomes in A but not B
Outcomes in neither A nor B
questions.correct_answer: Outcomes in both A and B
questions.explanation: Intersection corresponds to “and”.

questions.question: Aᶜ
options: A raised to the power c
The intersection of A and an event named c
All outcomes in Ω that are not in A
The number of outcomes in A
questions.correct_answer: All outcomes in Ω that are not in A
questions.explanation: The superscript c denotes complement relative to the chosen universe Ω.

questions.question: P(A)
options: The probability that event A occurs
The number of elements in A
questions.correct_answer: The probability that event A occurs
questions.explanation: P maps an event to its probability.

questions.question: P(A | B)
options: The probability of A or B
The probability of A divided by the probability of B
The probability of A given B
The probability of B given A
questions.correct_answer: The probability of A given B
questions.explanation: The vertical bar means “given”. The ratio P(A ∩ B) / P(B) requires P(B) > 0.

questions.question: |A|, for a finite set A
options: The length of every event A
The number of elements in A
questions.correct_answer: The number of elements in A
questions.explanation: Bars around a finite set denote cardinality: the number of elements in the set.

questions.question: {x | 0 ≤ x ≤ 1}
questions.correct_answer: Such that
questions.explanation: This describes the set of x such that the stated condition holds. It is set-builder notation, not conditional probability.

questions.question: [a, b], with a ≤ b
options: All real numbers strictly between a and b
Only the integers from a to b
All real numbers from a to b, including both endpoints
questions.correct_answer: All real numbers from a to b, including both endpoints
questions.explanation: Square brackets include the endpoints; braces {a, b} instead list just the endpoints.

questions.question: ℝ
options: The set of all probability laws
questions.correct_answer: The set of real numbers
questions.explanation: ℝ is the standard symbol for the set of real numbers.

questions.question: ℝ²
options: The probability of two independent events
The set of all ordered pairs of real numbers
A set containing exactly two numbers
The set of squares of real numbers
questions.correct_answer: The set of all ordered pairs of real numbers
questions.explanation: ℝ² is the real plane. Similarly, ℝ³ consists of triples and describes three-dimensional space.

questions.question: (x, y)
options: Only if x and y are integers
Only if x and y have equal probability
No: it means the same set as {x, y}
Yes: the first and second positions have different roles
questions.correct_answer: Yes: the first and second positions have different roles
questions.explanation: For two rolls, the first coordinate can record the first roll and the second the second roll.

options: Two independent events, by notation alone
All pairs (x, y) with both coordinates in [0, 1]
Only numbers obtained by multiplying the endpoints
Only the diagonal pairs with x = y
questions.correct_answer: All pairs (x, y) with both coordinates in [0, 1]
questions.explanation: This is a Cartesian product: the unit square. The symbol does not itself impose a probability law or independence.

questions.question: Aᵢ in A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ
options: A raised to the power i
Which event in the collection is meant
The probability of A multiplied by i
questions.correct_answer: Which event in the collection is meant
questions.explanation: A subscript labels an indexed event; it is not an exponent.

questions.question: ⋃ᵢ₌₁ⁿ Aᵢ
options: The intersection of A₁ through Aₙ
The set containing only the event Aₙ
The sum of the probabilities of A₁ through Aₙ
The union of A₁ through Aₙ
questions.correct_answer: The union of A₁ through Aₙ
questions.explanation: An outcome belongs to this union if it belongs to at least one indexed event.

questions.question: ⋂ᵢ₌₁ⁿ Aᵢ
options: The union of A₁ through Aₙ
The intersection of A₁ through Aₙ
questions.correct_answer: The intersection of A₁ through Aₙ
questions.explanation: An outcome belongs to this intersection if it belongs to every indexed event.

questions.question: Σᵢ₌₁³ pᵢ
questions.correct_answer: p₁ + p₂ + p₃
questions.explanation: The lower and upper limits specify the included indices; Σ means add the terms.

questions.question: ∏ᵢ₌₁³ pᵢ
questions.correct_answer: p₁ × p₂ × p₃
questions.explanation: ∏ means multiply the indexed terms. Multiplication of numbers is distinct from intersection of events.

questions.question: ⋃ᵢ₌₁^∞ Aᵢ
options: The union has probability greater than 1
There is one final event called A∞
Include every positive-integer index, without a finite last index
The events are indexed by every real number
questions.correct_answer: Include every positive-integer index, without a finite last index
questions.explanation: The notation specifies a countably infinite collection A₁, A₂, … . It does not specify its probability.

options: The set contains every real number
questions.correct_answer: The displayed pattern continues
questions.explanation: An ellipsis abbreviates the continuing pattern; here it lists the positive integers.

questions.question: n!
options: n multiplied by itself n times
questions.correct_answer: The product 1 × 2 × … × n
questions.explanation: The exclamation mark denotes factorial.
The convention 0! = 1 makes the counting formulas apply at boundary cases.

questions.question: C(n, k)
options: Unordered selections of k distinct objects from n distinct objects
All subsets of an n-element set, regardless of size
Selections of k objects allowing repeated choices
Ordered selections of k distinct objects from n distinct objects
questions.correct_answer: Unordered selections of k distinct objects from n distinct objects
questions.explanation: This binomial coefficient equals n!/[k!(n − k)!] for 0 ≤ k ≤ n.

questions.question: n! / (n₁! ··· nᵣ!)
options: Only the ways to choose the first group
Partitions where every ordering inside each group counts separately
All ordered arrangements of n objects without grouping
Ways to assign n distinct objects to labeled groups of sizes n₁, …, nᵣ
questions.correct_answer: Ways to assign n distinct objects to labeled groups of sizes n₁, …, nᵣ
questions.explanation: With nonnegative group sizes summing to n, the multinomial coefficient is n!/(n₁!…nᵣ!). Group labels matter; order within a group does not.

questions.question: |x − y|
options: The difference x − y, even when negative
The nonnegative distance between x and y
The probability of x given y
The number of elements in a set named x − y
questions.correct_answer: The nonnegative distance between x and y
questions.explanation: Bars around a number indicate absolute value, which gives the nonnegative distance between x and y.

questions.question: 0 ≤ x ≤ 1
options: x is between 0 and 1, including the endpoints
questions.correct_answer: x is between 0 and 1, including the endpoints
questions.explanation: ≤ means less than or equal to; ≥ means greater than or equal to. The signs < and > exclude equality.

questions.question: P(A ∩ B) ≠ P(A)P(B)
options: The two quantities are not equal
One of the probabilities is undefined
The left side is always larger
questions.correct_answer: The two quantities are not equal
questions.explanation: ≠ states inequality without specifying which side is larger.

questions.correct_answer: Approximately equal to
questions.explanation: ≈ indicates an approximate numerical equality.

questions.question: pᵏ
options: p multiplied by itself k times
The kth member of a collection p₁, p₂, …
questions.correct_answer: p multiplied by itself k times
questions.explanation: A superscript k is an exponent here; a subscript k would instead label a term.

questions.question: min(2, 4), max(2, 4)
questions.correct_answer: 2 and 4, respectively
questions.explanation: min selects the smaller value and max selects the larger value.

questions.question: p(k)
options: The probability of exactly k heads in all n tosses
The probability of a particular sequence with k heads
The probability of the kth toss being heads
questions.correct_answer: The probability of exactly k heads in all n tosses
questions.explanation: Parentheses indicate a function evaluated at k. This binomial probability counts all sequences containing exactly k heads.

questions.question: ∫ₛ dt, for S ⊆ [0, 1]
options: The probability of each individual point in S
The number of individual points in S
questions.correct_answer: The length of S
questions.explanation: This integrates the constant 1 over S. In a uniform model on [0, 1], the result is both the length of S and P(S).

questions.question: What is a sample space?
options: The set of equally likely outcomes
The set of all possible outcomes
The set of outcomes already observed
questions.correct_answer: The set of all possible outcomes
questions.explanation: A sample space lists what can happen. Equal likelihood is an extra assumption.

questions.question: What is an event?
options: The number of times an experiment is repeated
A subset of the sample space
questions.correct_answer: A subset of the sample space
questions.explanation: An event is a collection of outcomes; its probability is a separate quantity.

questions.question: A = {1, 2} and B = {2, 3}. What is A ∪ B?
questions.explanation: Union includes outcomes in either set, counting shared elements only once.

questions.question: A = {1, 2} and B = {2, 3}. What is A ∩ B?
questions.explanation: Intersection keeps only the outcomes shared by both sets.

questions.question: Ω = {1, 2, 3, 4} and A = {1, 4}. What is Aᶜ?
questions.explanation: The complement contains the outcomes in Ω that are not in A.

questions.question: When are A and B disjoint?
options: When neither event is a subset of the other
questions.correct_answer: When A ∩ B = ∅
questions.explanation: Disjoint events have no outcomes in common.

questions.question: Which collection partitions Ω = {1, 2, 3, 4}?
questions.explanation: A partition covers all of Ω with nonoverlapping sets.

questions.question: Which expression equals (A ∪ B)ᶜ?
questions.correct_answer: Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ
questions.explanation: Not being in either event means being outside both: de Morgan’s law.

questions.question: What two ingredients specify a probabilistic model?
options: A sample space and a probability law
A list of events and their observed counts
A sample space and equal probabilities for all outcomes
questions.correct_answer: A sample space and a probability law
questions.explanation: The sample space describes outcomes; the probability law assigns event probabilities.

questions.question: What must the outcomes in a sample space be?
questions.correct_answer: Mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive
questions.explanation: Exactly one listed outcome must occur whenever the experiment is performed.

questions.question: You toss a coin three times and want to know whether the first toss is heads. Is recording only the total number of heads sufficient?
options: Yes, if the coin is fair
No: a coin-toss sample space must be infinite
Yes: the total determines the first toss
questions.correct_answer: No: the order is lost
questions.explanation: For example, HTT and THT have the same number of heads but different first tosses.

questions.question: Which sample space is countably infinite?
options: The points inside a unit square
questions.explanation: The positive integers can be listed one by one. The real interval cannot; the coin space is finite.

questions.question: Which proposed outcome probabilities violate nonnegativity?
questions.explanation: A negative probability is invalid even when the numbers sum to 1.

questions.question: What is P(Ω)?
options: 1 divided by the number of outcomes
questions.explanation: Normalization assigns probability 1 to the entire sample space.

questions.question: A and B are disjoint, with P(A) = 0.2 and P(B) = 0.3. What is P(A ∪ B)?
questions.explanation: Additivity lets us add the probabilities of disjoint events.

questions.question: For a countably infinite sequence of disjoint events A₁, A₂, …, what is P(∪ᵢ Aᵢ)?
questions.correct_answer: Σᵢ P(Aᵢ)
questions.explanation: Countable additivity extends the disjoint-union rule to countably many events; their union need not be all of Ω.

questions.question: When does P(A) = |A| / |Ω| apply?
options: When Ω is finite and all its outcomes are equally likely
Whenever A and Aᶜ are disjoint
Whenever A contains more than one outcome
questions.correct_answer: When Ω is finite and all its outcomes are equally likely
questions.explanation: Counting outcomes is sufficient only under the discrete uniform law.

questions.question: If P(A) = 0.35, what is P(Aᶜ)?
questions.explanation: A and its complement partition Ω, so their probabilities sum to 1.

questions.question: P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. What is P(A ∪ B)?
questions.explanation: Add 0.6 and 0.5, then subtract the overlap 0.2 that was counted twice.

questions.question: Given only P(A) = 0.2 and P(B) = 0.3, what is the smallest guaranteed upper bound for P(A ∪ B)?
questions.explanation: The union bound gives at most 0.2 + 0.3. Disjoint events attain this bound.

questions.question: Ω = {a, b, c}, with probabilities 0.1, 0.3 and 0.6. What is P({a, c})?
questions.explanation: Add the probabilities of a and c; these outcomes are not equally likely.

questions.question: A point is chosen uniformly from [0, 1]. What is the probability that it lies in [0.2, 0.5]?
questions.explanation: For this uniform model, interval probability equals its length: 0.5 − 0.2.

questions.question: A point is chosen uniformly from [0, 1]. What is the probability of choosing exactly 0.5?
options: It cannot be assigned in this model
questions.explanation: A single point has zero length. In a continuous model, probability zero does not necessarily mean an empty event.

questions.question: A point (x, y) is chosen uniformly from the unit square. What is P(x + y ≤ 1)?
questions.explanation: The diagonal divides the square into two equal-area triangles; the event occupies one of them.

questions.question: For P(B) > 0, which formula defines P(A | B)?
questions.correct_answer: P(A ∩ B) / P(B)
questions.explanation: Conditioning retains the probability mass in B and renormalizes it to 1.

questions.question: If P(B) = 0, is P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B) defined?
questions.correct_answer: It is undefined
questions.explanation: The ratio would divide by zero, so this expression is undefined.

questions.question: A fair six-sided die shows an even number. What is the probability it shows 6?
questions.explanation: Only 2, 4 and 6 remain possible, and they are equally likely.

questions.question: Two independent fair coins are tossed. Given at least one head, what is the probability of two heads?
questions.explanation: The remaining equally likely outcomes are HH, HT and TH; only HH has two heads.

questions.question: A bag contains 3 red and 2 blue balls. Two balls are drawn uniformly without replacement. What is the probability both are red?
questions.explanation: Multiply 3/5 for the first red by 2/4 for the second red after the first is removed.

questions.question: A tree branch has probability 0.4. A following branch has conditional probability 0.3 given the first. What is the probability of the full path?
questions.explanation: Multiply the probabilities along the path: 0.4 × 0.3.

questions.question: When all conditioning events have positive probability, which formula always gives P(A ∩ B ∩ C)?
questions.correct_answer: P(A)P(B | A)P(C | A ∩ B)
questions.explanation: The chain rule conditions each stage on the entire preceding path; independence is not required.

questions.question: If P(A | B) = 0.7 and P(B) > 0, what is P(Aᶜ | B)?
questions.explanation: A conditional probability law also obeys the complement rule.

questions.question: A₁ and A₂ partition Ω and both have positive probability. Which expression gives P(B)?
questions.correct_answer: P(A₁)P(B | A₁) + P(A₂)P(B | A₂)
questions.explanation: Weight each conditional probability by the probability of its scenario.

questions.question: You face a beginner with probability 0.75 and an expert otherwise. Your win probabilities are 0.8 and 0.2 respectively. What is your overall win probability?
questions.explanation: Use total probability: 0.75 × 0.8 + 0.25 × 0.2 = 0.65.

questions.question: Machine A makes 60% of items and defects occur in 2% of its output. Machine B makes the rest with a 5% defect rate. What fraction of all items are defective?
questions.explanation: The weighted defect rate is 0.6 × 0.02 + 0.4 × 0.05 = 0.032.

questions.question: Machine A makes 60% of items with a 2% defect rate; B makes 40% with a 5% defect rate. Given a defective item, what is the probability it came from B?
questions.explanation: B contributes 0.4 × 0.05 = 0.02; all defects have probability 0.032. The ratio is 0.02/0.032 = 5/8.

questions.question: Does P(A | B) generally equal P(B | A)?
options: No: they condition on different events
Only when A and B are disjoint
Yes, whenever both probabilities are defined
questions.correct_answer: No: they condition on different events
questions.explanation: The numerators agree, but the denominators P(B) and P(A) can differ.

questions.question: A faulty device is selected with probability 0.01. An alarm sounds with probability 0.9 for faulty devices and 0.1 for working devices. Given an alarm, what is the probability the device is faulty?
questions.explanation: Fault-and-alarm probability is 0.009; total alarm probability is 0.009 + 0.099 = 0.108. Their ratio is 1/12.

questions.question: Assume P(A) > 0 and P(B) > 0. Which expression gives P(A | B) using Bayes’ rule?
questions.correct_answer: P(B | A)P(A) / P(B)
questions.explanation: Bayes’ rule reverses the conditioning using the prior P(A) and the evidence probability P(B).

questions.question: You know how common each cause is and how often each cause produces an observed signal. Which rule updates the probabilities of the causes after seeing the signal?
questions.correct_answer: Bayes’ rule
questions.explanation: The task is to infer a cause from evidence, which reverses the known conditional probabilities.

questions.question: Which equality defines independence of A and B?
questions.correct_answer: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)
questions.explanation: Independence is a factorization of the intersection probability, not a statement about overlap or equal probabilities.

questions.question: P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Are A and B independent?
options: Cannot be decided without knowing P(A ∪ B)
questions.correct_answer: Yes, since 0.2 = 0.4 × 0.5
questions.explanation: The product criterion holds exactly.

questions.question: A and B are disjoint and both have positive probability. Can they be independent?
questions.correct_answer: No
questions.explanation: Their intersection has probability 0, but P(A)P(B) is positive.

questions.question: A and B are independent, P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A ∩ Bᶜ)?
questions.explanation: A is also independent of Bᶜ, so the probability is 0.3 × 0.6.

questions.question: For P(C) > 0, which equality defines independence of A and B conditional on C?
options: P(A ∩ B | C) = P(A | C) + P(B | C)
P(A ∩ B | C) = P(A | C)P(B | C)
questions.correct_answer: P(A ∩ B | C) = P(A | C)P(B | C)
questions.explanation: Conditional independence uses probabilities under the same conditional law.

questions.question: How are independence and conditional independence related in general?
options: They are equivalent whenever the conditioning event has positive probability
questions.correct_answer: Neither implies the other
questions.explanation: Learning additional information can create or remove dependence; both directions have counterexamples.

questions.question: Is pairwise independence of three events enough to guarantee mutual independence?
options: Only when all three have probability 1/2
Only when their probabilities add to 1
questions.correct_answer: No
questions.explanation: Mutual independence also requires the three-event intersection to factor.

questions.question: Two independent fair coins are tossed. Let A = first toss is heads, B = second toss is heads, and C = tosses differ. Are A, B and C mutually independent?
options: No: mutual independence requires the events to be disjoint
No: the triple intersection has probability 0, not 1/8
questions.correct_answer: No: the triple intersection has probability 0, not 1/8
questions.explanation: Each event has probability 1/2, but A ∩ B ∩ C is empty. Pairwise independence is insufficient.

questions.question: What describes a sequence of independent Bernoulli trials?
options: Any repeated experiment, even if outcomes affect later trials
Independent two-outcome trials with the same success probability
Trials with exactly one success overall
Independent trials that must each have success probability 1/2
questions.correct_answer: Independent two-outcome trials with the same success probability
questions.explanation: A Bernoulli sequence consists of identical independent stages, each labeled success or failure.

questions.question: A coin has P(H) = 0.6 on each independent toss. What is the probability of the specific sequence HHT?
questions.explanation: A specific sequence has probability 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.4. Do not multiply by the number of other sequences.

questions.question: How many sequences of four coin tosses contain exactly two heads?
questions.explanation: Choose the two head positions: C(4, 2) = 6. The order of heads and tails distinguishes sequences.

questions.question: For four independent fair coin tosses, what is the probability of exactly two heads?
questions.explanation: There are 6 qualifying sequences, each with probability 1/16, giving 6/16 = 3/8.

questions.question: A trial succeeds with probability 0.2. Across three independent trials, what is the probability of at least one success?
questions.explanation: Subtract the probability of no successes: 1 − 0.8³ = 0.488.

questions.question: Each of three users independently needs a connection with probability 1/2. A system has two connections. What is the probability demand exceeds capacity?
questions.explanation: Demand exceeds two only when all three need a connection: (1/2)³.

questions.question: Two independent components work with probabilities 0.9 and 0.8. A system needs both to work. What is its success probability?
questions.explanation: For a series system, multiply the component success probabilities.

questions.question: Two independent components work with probabilities 0.9 and 0.8. A system needs at least one to work. What is its success probability?
questions.explanation: A parallel system fails only if both fail: success probability is 1 − 0.1 × 0.2.

questions.question: A code has one of 3 letters followed by one of 4 digits. How many codes are possible?
questions.explanation: The choices form two stages: 3 × 4 = 12.

questions.question: How many subsets does a set with 5 elements have, including ∅ and the whole set?
questions.explanation: Each of the five elements is either included or excluded, giving 2⁵ subsets.

questions.question: In how many orders can 4 distinct books be arranged in a row?
questions.explanation: Arrange all four distinct objects: 4! = 24.

questions.question: From 5 people, choose a president and a different secretary. How many assignments are possible?
questions.explanation: The roles are distinct and no person fills both: 5 × 4 = 20.

questions.question: How many unordered teams of 2 can be chosen from 5 people?
questions.explanation: Order does not matter: C(5, 2) = 5!/(2!3!) = 10.

questions.question: Which formula counts ordered selections of k distinct objects from n distinct objects, without replacement (0 ≤ k ≤ n)?
questions.explanation: Ordering matters and repetitions are forbidden, so use k-permutations.

questions.question: Six distinct people are assigned to labeled groups A, B and C, with 2 people per group. How many assignments are possible?
questions.explanation: Use the multinomial count 6!/(2!2!2!) = 90. The group labels matter; within-group order does not.

questions.question: How many distinct letter sequences can be formed by rearranging LEVEL?
questions.explanation: There are five letters, with L repeated twice and E twice: 5!/(2!2!) = 30.
